To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) tephra layers from the same eruption are found in three Neogene sedimentary basins in the western United States that are spatially separated by hundreds of kilometers and (2) the ages of the tephra layers are consistent with a model in which the North American Plate is moving over a hotspot that is spreading out from a point source.
the basins in eastern Idaho and northwestern Wyoming experienced pulses of extension separated in time and space that are related to the migration of a hotspot.

the late Miocene and Pliocene extensional basins of eastern Idaho and Wyoming record discrete pulses of activity that are staggered in time and spatially separated, which is consistent with a west-to-east migration of extension related to the Yellowstone plume.

the relationship of tephra deposits to the evolution of the Yellowstone hotspot and its associated volcanic and structural features.
establishing a chronology of the late Neogene extension in the northern Rocky Mountains, the tectonic setting for which has long been a subject of debate.
the timing and spatial distribution of extension and tectonic events in the western United States and how they relate to the Yellowstone hotspot track and its associated volcanism.

the tephra record from the three basins is consistent with the model of the Yellowstone hotspot and its migration across the North American continent.
